clue.text: Pop star, speaking drunkenly, invented language

indicators.note: a drunk slurs a final S into SH, so the name is said with a lisping slur

parts.note: Elvis Presley, the singer known simply by his first name

explanation.surface: A tipsy fan slurs the King's name, and somehow coins a new tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Slur the S of ELVIS the way a drunk would and it comes out with an SH ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien constructed a tongue for his elves in The Lord of the Rings, a famous artificial language.

clue.text: Dreamer in dunce's cap is teased

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A daydreaming pupil in a dunce's cap is mocked.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who retreats into fantasy to avoid reality is a daydreamer.

clue.text: Greenery from a fen with vile ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed, so the letters are mashed into a new order

explanation.surface: Plants from a marsh mashed with something nasty.
explanation.definitionFit: The foliage of the grape plant, used in dolmades, is green leafy matter.

clue.text: Cool Greek stores with ices reduced by 50%

indicators.note: cut in half, so only the first half of each word stays

explanation.surface: A calm Greek shopkeeper's stock of ices has been halved.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Zeno's Athenian school bore pain unmoved, hence a calm, unflappable person.

clue.text: Cameron admits English ruined Welsh port

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so one letter goes inside the other piece

parts.note: David Cameron was Prime Minister, abbreviated PM
ruined financially means broke

explanation.surface: A former prime minister confesses that an Englishman wrecked a Welsh harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: Cameron here stands for his office, PM, rather than any name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pembroke Dock is a harbour town in south-west Wales, with ferries to Ireland.

clue.text: Reasonable age for people to get gentle hint, doddering about

indicators.note: about means around, so the shuffled letters surround the next piece
tottering unsteadily, so the letters stumble into a new order

parts.note: men is a word for people

explanation.surface: Elderly people, wobbling about, get a gentle nudge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reasonable age' looks like a person's sensible years, but it is the historical period; 'doddering' makes ENLIGHTENT, which 'about' wraps round the people.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century Age of Reason, when rational thought was prized, is its historical name.

clue.text: Fruit cups Elizabeth returned with loaf

parts.note: a bra is made of cups

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the name runs backwards

parts.note: Liz is short for Elizabeth
loaf and nut are both slang for the head

explanation.surface: A dessert bowl, Elizabeth brought back with a loaf of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' is slang for head (as in 'use your loaf'), as is 'nut'.
explanation.definitionFit: A large South American seed in a hard shell is botanically and in shops sold as a fruit.

clue.text: What the experts know about particles

parts.note: on means concerning, about
ions are charged particles

explanation.surface: What specialists understand concerning particle physics.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert is said to 'know their onions', the idiom for knowing a subject thoroughly.

clue.text: Blackmail's no longer wrong?

parts.note: ex means former, no longer
a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Is blackmail no longer considered a crime?
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain by threats or coercion is what a blackmailer does, so the verbs coincide.

clue.text: Tory Party accommodation

parts.note: CON is short for Conservative, the Tory party
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A Conservative gathering provides somewhere to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment in a block owned unit by unit, the American short form of condominium, is a type of housing.

clue.text: Bourbon intoxicated relations

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters of the next word reel into a new order

explanation.surface: Drunken family members after a glass of bourbon whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: Bourbon looks like the whiskey, but it is the French royal house.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orleanist faction backed the Orléans branch of the French royal house of Bourbon, so a supporter is a kind of Bourbon loyalist.

clue.text: Corrupt world OK by Eton — it's how Etonians thrive!

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or warped, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A rotten world approved by Eton, the means by which its pupils prosper.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is England's most famous private school, whose alumni have run much of public life.
explanation.definitionFit: Former pupils of elite schools help one another into jobs; that mutual favouritism is how they get ahead.

clue.text: Explorer receives very cool tip from Guatemalan tracker

indicators.note: receives means takes in, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: Marco Polo, the Venetian traveller
iced means chilled, very cool

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An explorer gets an icy piece of advice from a Central American guide.
explanation.definitionFit: A trained police animal follows scents to find suspects, so it is a tracker.

clue.text: A reprobate abandoned by society, Archer could aim for this

indicators.note: abandoned by means left without, so the letter for society drops out

parts.note: a reprobate is a wrongdoer, a sinner

explanation.surface: A villain shunned by polite company, a target for an archer.
explanation.definitionFit: On an archery target, the ring just outside the bull is the one a bowman might aim at.

clue.text: Special walk, one in Chamonix, gets strength circulating in an arm and a leg

indicators.note: moving around within, so this piece goes into the middle of the others

parts.note: a mall is a shaded walk, as in Pall Mall
UNE is French for one, and Chamonix is a French ski resort
FORT is a strong point, a strength

explanation.surface: A special hike in the Alps gets the blood circulating through your limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An arm and a leg' looks like body parts, but it is the idiom for a huge price.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that costs an arm and a leg is very expensive, an idiom for a large sum of money.

clue.text: Revolutionary comrade I saw getting stoned

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the friend word runs backwards

parts.note: a pal is a friend, a comrade
to see someone romantically is to date them, so saw means went out with

explanation.surface: A revolutionary comrade admits seeing people get high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting stoned' suggests drugs, but it means pelted with rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: To lapidate is to pelt with rocks, an old word for execution by rocks thrown.

clue.text: Is Picaroon working without scrap of hope?

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the other pieces surround the scrap

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself would say 'am I'
a bit is a scrap
on means working, in operation

explanation.surface: Is the setter at work with no shred of optimism left?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the old sense outside, not lacking; Picaroon is the setter of this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong desire to achieve something is an aspiration, a hope for the future.

clue.text: Saint included by diviner religious composer

indicators.note: included by means held within, so the saint goes inside the diviner

parts.note: a palmist tells fortunes from hands

explanation.surface: A saint consulted a fortune-teller about a hymn writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of sacred songs, such as King David, writes religious music.

clue.text: Looking in the paper to see when you can buy a drink

definitions.meaning: opening The Times newspaper to read it

definitions.text: when you can buy a drink
definitions.meaning: the hours a pub is licensed to serve

explanation.surface: Checking the newspaper to find out when the pub opens.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the phrase as opening The Times, the London daily.
explanation.definitionFit: Licensed premises post the hours they are trading, and opening The Times is literally browsing a newspaper.

clue.text: Charm Hanoverian king repeatedly

indicators.note: repeatedly means the piece appears twice

parts.note: George I, the first Hanoverian king, is GR I, Georgius Rex the first

explanation.surface: The first Georgian king keeps casting a spell.
explanation.definitionFit: A West African amulet worn to ward off evil is a talisman, a charm.

clue.text: Spaniards here struggled to break scoreless draw

indicators.note: to break means to split open, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a nil-nil result, written as two zeros, OO
vied means competed, struggled

explanation.surface: Spanish footballers fought hard to break a goalless deadlock.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in Asturias, northern Spain, is a place where Spanish people live.

clue.text: Did party welcome Democrat after Republican?

indicators.note: after puts the welcome and Democrat behind the Republican

parts.note: ave is a Latin greeting, hail

explanation.surface: Did the party welcome a Democrat following a Republican?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political beside the US parties, but here it is a verb for going out dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: To rave is to party wildly, so went partying fits the past tense.

clue.text: Time to study utilitarian but it's a dreary experience

parts.note: to read a subject at university is to study it
John Stuart Mill, the utilitarian philosopher

explanation.surface: Time spent reading a utilitarian philosopher is a tedious slog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read' for 'study' is the British university usage: you read history.
explanation.definitionFit: A monotonous routine is figuratively a grind on a moving belt, a dull repetitive experience.

clue.text: Went for the green finish on household range

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its last letter

parts.note: to range is to wander, rove

explanation.surface: A golfer heads for the green, finishing on a domestic driving range.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf you drive towards the green, so 'went for the green' is drove.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer hitting a long tee shot at the putting surface has struck a drive.

clue.text: A cottage gets plastered, keeping right winter protection

indicators.note: keeping means holding within, so one letter goes inside
plastered means drunk, so the letters lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: A cottage gets a coat of plaster, staying snug through winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets plastered' turns ACOTTAGE into GEATCOAT, and 'keeping' puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy overcoat, especially a military one, guards against cold weather.

clue.text: Current writer rejected African bounder

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
a Biro is a ballpoint pen

explanation.surface: An electric current writer turns down an African cad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounder' looks like a cad, but it is an animal that bounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A small antelope of the African savanna that leaps as it runs is aptly a bounding creature.

clue.text: I dunk crackers in caviar for military leader

indicators.note: in puts the shuffled letters inside the caviar

parts.note: caviar is fish eggs, roe

indicators.note: crackers means mad, so the letters go haywire

explanation.surface: Dipping crackers into caviar to feed a general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crackers' looks like biscuits for dunking, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Wellington, victor at Waterloo, was nicknamed for his firmness: a famous general.

clue.text: What's in cheese, note, comes from the east

indicators.note: in an across entry, coming from the east means running right to left

parts.note: a tenner is a ten-pound note

explanation.surface: A cheese-loving tourist's banknote travels from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: Curdled milk for cheese is set with an enzyme taken from calves' stomachs.
